title: The Private Markets Tech Stack (Part 3): Why Now
summary: Part 3 on private markets tech consolidation: which layers are worth owning, and why it's happening now.
body_markdown:
*Part 2 covered why an AI layer on top of fragmented systems doesn’t work, and how Mantle Portal built its data foundation from ingestion up through accounting. This final part looks at which layers of the stack are actually worth owning, why this shift is happening now, and what becomes possible once the data underneath is finally trustworthy.*


---


## Where the line holds


Not every layer of this stack is worth owning, and the platforms that win this next phase of consolidation won’t be the ones that try to replace everything. Institutions have run custodian feed infrastructure for 15+ years, and there’s little appetite to rip it out, because it was never the bottleneck. The same is true of performance and reporting engines, which are deeply embedded and contractually entrenched across asset classes. Those systems aren’t where the industry’s next fight is happening.


The layer actually worth owning sits in between: what happens after the feed arrives and before a trustworthy number reaches someone who can act on it. That’s where the breakdown has always occurred, and it’s the layer a unified data model is built to close. By becoming the connective tissue between the tools institutions already run, cross-portfolio questions those tools were never designed to answer finally get answered.


The accounting layer is the clearest test of where that boundary sits. A platform that only reports numbers has a fundamentally different relationship to the ledger than one that produces the accounting consequence itself. Mantle Portal generates the journal entry; the incumbent ledger still persists it. That distinction – who produces the consequence versus who simply stores it – is likely to matter more than any single vendor’s feature list as this market consolidates. It’s the difference between a tool institutions can route around and one they can’t.


Payment execution is the same pattern showing up one layer downstream. Capital calls, approvals, and payment instructions have historically lived apart from the system tracking the underlying portfolio: an LP reviews a call in one tool, approves it over email, and executes the wire in a bank portal. With Dream Payments powering execution inside Mantle Portal, data, documents, approval workflow, and payment execution now sit in one system. It’s an earlier proof point than the accounting engine, but it points in the same direction of travel: infrastructure that coordinates what happens to the money, not just infrastructure that reports on it afterward.


That unified foundation pays off in a place dashboards can’t follow. A dashboard reports numbers someone already decided to compute; inference answers a question nobody wrote a report for. That’s only possible now because the data underneath is finally trustworthy. Ask “what was my best investment?” and instead of a multi-week project netting cash flows across vintages, currencies, and co-investment structures, it’s a query. Ask “what should I buy more of?”, a forward-looking judgement call about sector concentration, correlation with existing exposures, and unused GP capacity, and Mantle Portal can reason across the whole portfolio because it finally lives in one place. Neither question is new, and institutions have always wanted both answered. What’s new is that a question that used to take ten weeks can now be asked as often as it matters, not just at the quarterly review.


---


## Why this is happening now


The broader market is validating the same read, from two directions at once.


In July 2026, Bloomberg announced its plans to acquire Canoe Intelligence, a data extraction and normalization platform built specifically for alternative investment documents, folding it into Bloomberg’s portfolio and risk analytics offering. A player with Bloomberg’s resources and reach didn’t need to build extraction from scratch, but instead chose to buy a specialist rather than bolt on a shallow version internally, which says something about how hard that layer actually is to get right. It signals that a large, well-resourced player has concluded point solutions have value, but are not the permanent solution and live amongst a broader toolset.


The opposite data point from an equally well-resourced player, and it’s just as telling. Anthropic’s Claude for Financial Advisors, announced September 14, connects Claude to custodians, CRMs, and wealth-tech providers rather than replacing or unifying them — the assistant-on-top approach, built by the company arguably best equipped to build it well. Read the two moves side by side and the direction of travel gets clearer, not murkier: one large player bought its way into owning more of the data lifecycle, the other shipped the fastest thing that could plausibly help this quarter. Both are rational bets. Only one of them closes the gap this whole series has been describing.


Mantle Portal’s approach also wasn’t a rip-and-replace of what institutions already run. It stood up a normalization layer alongside the existing stack, one indifferent to fifteen years of downstream customization because it ingests, normalizes, and delivers clean data outward regardless of what sits downstream. Once clean data is flowing, the old workarounds become redundant on their own terms rather than requiring a political fight over whose workflow gets deprecated. That’s a more realistic adoption path for large institutions than any pitch that starts with “replace everything.”


Four layers: ledger, ingestion and extraction, analytics and reporting, and CRM, unified on a single data model. That unification is what finally lets an institution ask a real question about its own portfolio and get a trustworthy answer back the same day, instead of the multi-week project it used to be. That’s the architecture we built while the rest of the industry was still deciding whether consolidation was coming. It already arrived.
